International Building Code, section 903.2.8: automatic sprinklers throughout buildings with a Group R fire area (NFPA 13R allowed in low-rise residential)

parameters.rationale: Code threshold: a duplex is built under the residential code; three or more homes in one building are built under the building code, which requires sprinklers, rated walls and floors between homes and a fire alarm. The amount per square foot is a judgement, flagged as such; the threshold itself is the cited code scope. Pennsylvania adopts both codes through its Uniform Construction Code.
parameters.revisit: Price NFPA 13R systems and rated assemblies from Pennsylvania small-building bids.

parameters.label: Added required return for buildings of five or more homes (commercial financing)

source.citation: Fannie Mae Selling Guide: residential mortgages cover one- to four-unit properties; five or more units need a multifamily (commercial) loan

parameters.rationale: Financing threshold: a building of up to four homes can be bought with a residential mortgage, often by an owner who lives in one home; five or more homes need a commercial loan with lower loan-to-value, a debt-service test and shorter terms. The builder's required return rises by this much over the base margin. The size is a judgement, flagged as such.
parameters.revisit: Compare small-balance multifamily loan terms with 2-4 unit mortgage terms.

parameters.label: Existing homes removed per project
parameters.rationale: Each project is assumed to replace one existing single-family home, so net units = new units - 1.
parameters.revisit: Allow for vacant-lot projects (0 removed) once lot data allow it.

parameters.label: Demolition and site clearance per redeveloped lot
parameters.rationale: Taking down a house, abating older materials, capping utilities and clearing the lot. The benchmark folds this into the soft-cost share; the prototype comparison shows it as its own line.
parameters.revisit: Sample demolition permit valuations in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh permit files.

parameters.label: Builder profit required, as a share of total cost
parameters.rationale: Small builders typically need 10-20% on cost to take on a project.
parameters.revisit: Source from published feasibility studies of small multi-unit buildings.

parameters.label: Share of missing-middle units that replace baseline construction
parameters.rationale: Some builders would have built single-family homes or apartments elsewhere instead.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from hindcast places.

parameters.label: Share of those lots large enough for a 2-6 unit building
parameters.rationale: Setbacks and coverage are assumed not to bind (Handbook), so lot area and shape decide.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from the block lot-size proxy and parcel counties.

parameters.label: Share of homes with no mapped sewer record that have municipal water and sewer
parameters.rationale: Used only where a state floor depends on service. A home outside every mapped sewer service area is "unknown", not "unserved", because the map lists service areas but does not claim to be complete; most such homes are on septic systems, so only a small share is taken as served. Team judgement.
parameters.revisit: Replace when a complete service inventory or a water layer is in the pack.

parameters.label: Share of homes inside a mapped municipal sewer area also on municipal water
parameters.rationale: Used only where a state floor depends on service (Vermont's 24 V.S.A. § 4412(1)(D): up to four units only where municipal water AND sewer serve). The pack maps sewer service areas but has no statewide municipal water map, so whether a sewered home also has municipal water is not known. Village and town-centre sewer systems are usually paired with a public water system; the low end allows for sewered areas on private wells. Team judgement.
parameters.revisit: Replace with a mapped public water service layer when one is added to the pack.

parameters.label: Construction cost per square foot, 2-6 unit building
parameters.rationale: Wood-frame small multifamily building; wide range for region and finish.
parameters.revisit: Look for a free public construction cost source.

parameters.label: Share of block land per home that is the home's own lot
parameters.rationale: The block lot-size proxy divides a block's land by its homes, so it also counts half the streets, parks and shops. Lot area = proxy x this share.
parameters.revisit: Compare the proxy with parcel areas in Tier 2 counties.

parameters.label: Tallest building the reform allows

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

parameters.rationale: The Handbook allows building heights up to three stories.
parameters.revisit: Only if the Handbook changes.

parameters.label: Most units the reform allows on a lot

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

parameters.rationale: The Handbook allows 2-6 dwelling units on parcels currently restricted to single-family use.
parameters.revisit: Only if the Handbook changes.

parameters.label: Smallest lot that holds a 2-6 unit building
parameters.rationale: With setbacks and coverage not binding (Handbook), a three-storey building of 2-6 units of about 1,000 sq ft plus surface parking needs roughly 3,500-7,000 sq ft of lot. Used only when the tract has the block lot-size proxy.
parameters.revisit: Measure built missing-middle lot sizes in Tier 2 parcel counties.

parameters.label: Fewest units the reform allows on a lot

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

parameters.rationale: The Handbook allows 2-6 dwelling units on parcels currently restricted to single-family use.
parameters.revisit: Only if the Handbook changes.

parameters.label: Rent premium of a new 2-6 unit building's homes over the census two-bedroom median
parameters.rationale: Census medians mix long-time tenants in older buildings with new leases. A newly built apartment of about 1,000 sq ft usually asks well above the median two-bedroom rent of its tract, more so than a small backyard ADU (adu.new_unit_rent_premium), so this entry is its own.
parameters.revisit: Compare Census SOMA asking rents for new apartments with ACS median gross rent.

parameters.label: Operating costs as a share of rent, 2-6 unit building
parameters.rationale: Vacancy, management, upkeep, insurance and property tax for a small rental building.
parameters.revisit: Build from parts as for ADUs.

parameters.label: Smallest lot for a duplex prototype
parameters.rationale: Two homes side by side or stacked fit on a typical older city or inner suburban lot. Read with missing_middle.lot_proxy_net_share against the block land per home.
parameters.revisit: Measure from parcel maps of duplexes built since 2015.

parameters.label: Floor area per home, duplex prototype
parameters.rationale: Duplex homes are usually three-bedroom family homes, larger than flats in bigger buildings.
parameters.revisit: Check against new two-unit building permits (floor area per unit).

parameters.label: Smallest lot for a fourplex prototype
parameters.rationale: Four homes in three storeys with surface parking need a wider or deeper lot than a duplex.
parameters.revisit: Measure from parcel maps of fourplexes built since 2015.

parameters.label: Floor area per home, fourplex prototype
parameters.rationale: Two-bedroom flats, the common fourplex layout.
parameters.revisit: Check against new 3-4 unit building permits (floor area per unit).

parameters.label: Smallest lot for a six-unit prototype (up to three storeys)
parameters.rationale: Six homes in three storeys with surface parking need about two typical single-family lots.
parameters.revisit: Measure from parcel maps of five- and six-unit buildings built since 2015.

parameters.label: Floor area per home, six-unit prototype
parameters.rationale: One- and two-bedroom flats, so six homes fit in three storeys on a double lot.
parameters.revisit: Check against new 5+ unit small-building permits (floor area per unit).

parameters.label: Missing-middle permits in the first year, as a share of the steady rate
parameters.rationale: Builders must learn the new rules, find sites and arrange money, so the first year is slow; the rate climbs to full over missing_middle.ramp_years_to_full.
parameters.revisit: Fit to published post-reform permit paths.

parameters.label: Years for missing-middle permits to reach the steady yearly rate
parameters.rationale: Builders need time to learn new rules and assemble sites; slower than ADUs.
parameters.revisit: Fit to published post-reform permit paths.

parameters.label: Share of feasible lots redeveloped each year
parameters.rationale: Redevelopment needs a sale and a builder, so it is rare: well under 1% of feasible lots a year. Early results of gentle-density reforms were small.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on places with gentle-density reforms and published permits.

parameters.label: Two-bedroom rent as a share of the all-unit median rent (fallback)
parameters.rationale: A missing-middle unit of about 1,000 sq ft rents like a two-bedroom. The tract's own two-bedroom median is used where it exists; this ratio times the tract's median gross rent is the fallback where it is blank.
parameters.revisit: Compute county ratios from ACS B25031 as for the one-bedroom ratio.

parameters.label: Three-bedroom rent as a multiple of two-bedroom rent (where the three-bedroom median is blank)
parameters.rationale: The duplex prototype rents as a three-bedroom home. Where the tract's three-bedroom median is blank, its two-bedroom rent times this ratio stands in.
parameters.revisit: Fit from ACS B25031 county medians (three-bedroom over two-bedroom).

parameters.label: Share of single-family lots in single-family-only zones
parameters.rationale: Most single-family homes sit in zones that allow nothing else; older boroughs and cities often allow two units already.
parameters.revisit: Replace with zoning data in Tier 2 counties and the town-rule index.

parameters.label: Share of single-family homes sold each year
parameters.rationale: A lot is redeveloped only after it is sold, so the yearly redevelopment rate can never exceed the yearly sale rate of single-family homes. The funnel uses the smaller of the two in every draw.
parameters.revisit: Source from county deed-transfer counts or a published home-sales series.

parameters.label: Soft costs as a share of construction, 2-6 unit building
parameters.rationale: Design, permits, financing and fees (other than the benchmark fee) for a small project.
parameters.revisit: Source from published development pro formas.

parameters.label: Years after January 1, 2027 before missing-middle permits start to respond
parameters.rationale: The benchmark reform is assumed to be in force on the first day of the window; the slow start is in the ramp (missing_middle.ramp_first_year_share).
parameters.revisit: Set from a bill's effective date when a bill is modelled.

parameters.label: Relative weight of duplexes (2 units) in the missing-middle mix
parameters.rationale: The funnel prices five building types, from a duplex to a sixplex, and weights them. The five weights are drawn and then divided by their sum, so only their relative size matters. Duplexes are the most common gentle-density project in places that allow them, because they need the least land and money.
parameters.revisit: Set from permits by structure type in places after gentle-density reforms.

parameters.label: Relative weight of five-unit buildings in the missing-middle mix
parameters.rationale: Five or more units usually moves a building to commercial financing and stricter building-code rules, so five-unit buildings are rare. Weights are divided by their sum.
parameters.revisit: Set from permits by structure type in places after gentle-density reforms.

parameters.label: Relative weight of fourplexes (4 units) in the missing-middle mix
parameters.rationale: Fourplexes are the largest building that many lenders still finance as residential; a common middle case. Weights are divided by their sum.
parameters.revisit: Set from permits by structure type in places after gentle-density reforms.

parameters.label: Relative weight of sixplexes (6 units) in the missing-middle mix
parameters.rationale: If a builder moves to commercial rules anyway, the most units allowed pay best, so sixplexes are more common than five-unit buildings. Weights are divided by their sum.
parameters.revisit: Set from permits by structure type in places after gentle-density reforms.

parameters.label: Relative weight of triplexes (3 units) in the missing-middle mix
parameters.rationale: Second most common small form; weights are divided by their sum in every draw.
parameters.revisit: Set from permits by structure type in places after gentle-density reforms.

parameters.label: Floor area per missing-middle unit
parameters.rationale: Units in small multi-unit buildings are typically two-bedroom homes of about 1,000 sq ft.
parameters.revisit: Check against new small multifamily construction data.

parameters.label: Units in a typical missing-middle project
parameters.rationale: Projects range from duplexes to sixplexes; fourplexes are a common middle case.
parameters.revisit: Check against permits by structure type in places after gentle-density reforms.

parameters.label: Capitalisation rate used to value a finished mid-rise building
parameters.rationale: Larger, newer apartment buildings trade at somewhat lower cap rates than small ones.
parameters.revisit: Source from a published cap-rate survey for Pennsylvania metros.

parameters.label: Developer profit required on a mid-rise project, as a share of total cost
parameters.rationale: Developers and their investors typically need 10-20% on cost for larger projects.
parameters.revisit: Source from published feasibility studies.

parameters.label: Construction cost per square foot, mid-rise apartment building
parameters.rationale: Wood or light-steel frame over a concrete podium costs more per square foot than small buildings; the range covers region and finish.
parameters.revisit: Look for a free public construction cost source.

parameters.label: Operating costs as a share of rent, mid-rise apartment building
parameters.rationale: Vacancy, management, upkeep, insurance and property tax for a professionally run building.
parameters.revisit: Build from parts as for ADUs.

parameters.label: Soft costs as a share of construction, mid-rise apartment building
parameters.rationale: Design, permits, financing and other soft costs (other than the benchmark fee).
parameters.revisit: Source from published development pro formas.

parameters.label: Floor area per mid-rise apartment
parameters.rationale: New mid-rise apartments are mostly studios to two-bedrooms averaging about 850 sq ft.
parameters.revisit: Check against new multifamily construction characteristics (Census SOC).

parameters.label: Units in a typical mid-rise apartment project
parameters.rationale: Four- to six-storey buildings near transit stops typically hold a few dozen to about 150 apartments.
parameters.revisit: Check against permits for 5+ unit buildings in Pennsylvania metros.

parameters.label: Cost of one space in an above-ground parking structure

source.citation: UCLA Institute of Transportation Studies (February 2026), "No Such Thing as Free Parking", construction cost per space from 2025 Rider Levett Bucknall cost data for 17 U.S. cities, excluding land

parameters.rationale: Above-ground structures averaged about $52,000 per space across 17 cities, from $29,000 (Phoenix, Washington DC) to $99,000 (Portland), excluding land.
parameters.revisit: Check whether Philadelphia or Pittsburgh is among the 17 cities and use its value.

parameters.label: Cost of one surface parking space, land and construction

source.citation: Victoria Transport Policy Institute, Transportation Cost and Benefit Analysis II, chapter 5.4 "Parking Costs" (version of 3 October 2022), Table 5.4.4-1

parameters.rationale: The review's summary table puts surface parking land and construction at about $8,000 per space in 2022 dollars. Low covers cheap rural land; high covers urban land.
parameters.revisit: Update the price year to 2026 and check against a Pennsylvania cost estimate.

parameters.label: Cost of one underground parking space

source.citation: UCLA Institute of Transportation Studies (February 2026), "No Such Thing as Free Parking", construction cost per space from 2025 Rider Levett Bucknall cost data for 17 U.S. cities, excluding land

parameters.rationale: Underground parking averaged about $73,000 per space across 17 cities, from $40,000 (Washington DC) to $111,000 (Portland), excluding land.
parameters.revisit: Check whether Philadelphia or Pittsburgh is among the 17 cities and use its value.

parameters.label: Share of spaces in structures, other tracts
parameters.rationale: Outside dense areas almost all residential parking is surface or garage parking.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from local project data or land prices.

parameters.label: Share of spaces in above-ground structures, transit-rich tracts
parameters.rationale: Where land is dear, more parking is stacked in structures; the rest is surface or underground.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from local project data or land prices.

parameters.label: Share of spaces that are surface spaces, 2-4-unit buildings
parameters.rationale: Small buildings park on driveways and small lots; the rest are tuck-under garages, costed as structured spaces.
parameters.revisit: Check against a sample of new 2-4-unit buildings in Pennsylvania.

parameters.label: Share of spaces underground, other tracts
parameters.rationale: Away from transit, underground residential parking is very rare.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from local project data or land prices.

parameters.label: Share of spaces underground, transit-rich tracts
parameters.rationale: Underground parking is mostly limited to large projects in the densest places.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from local project data or land prices.

parameters.label: Share of formerly required spaces still built, no-response case (variant)
parameters.rationale: The explicit no-response case: builders keep providing every space the old minimum required, so the reform saves nothing and adds nothing. Used only by the variant 'parking_no_response'.
parameters.revisit: None; this is a bounding case.

parameters.label: First-year permit response to the parking reform as a share of the full yearly response
parameters.rationale: Projects must be redesigned with fewer spaces before the saving shows in a permit, so the first year is slower than for a fee cut. Shapes the years only; the five-year total is unchanged.
parameters.revisit: Check against permit paths after parking-minimum repeals (Buffalo, Minneapolis).

parameters.label: Years for the permit response to the parking reform to reach its full yearly level
parameters.rationale: Redesign, site plans and financing take one to three years after a rule change.
parameters.revisit: Check against permit paths after parking-minimum repeals.

parameters.label: Parking spaces required per townhouse or small multi-unit home
parameters.rationale: Townhouse and two-to-four-unit minimums are usually one to two spaces per unit.
parameters.revisit: Replace with a sample of Pennsylvania zoning codes.

parameters.label: Parking spaces required per apartment under current rules
parameters.rationale: Common local minimums for apartments are one to two spaces per unit.
parameters.revisit: Replace with a sample of Pennsylvania zoning codes.

parameters.label: Share of formerly required spaces still built, other tracts
parameters.rationale: Away from transit, most projects keep building close to the old minimum (85-100%), so the saving is small.
parameters.revisit: Cite the post-reform studies of what developers built.

parameters.label: Share of formerly required spaces still built, transit-rich tracts
parameters.rationale: After minimums are removed, projects near frequent transit still build about 60% of the spaces once required, because lenders and buyers still want parking.
parameters.revisit: Cite the post-reform studies of what developers built.

parameters.label: Extra units a small site can hold when parking is not required
parameters.rationale: Land no longer needed for parking can hold more homes on tight sites. The gain is small on average and zero where land is plentiful.
parameters.revisit: Test with the pro forma on typical lot sizes; cite site-yield studies.

parameters.label: Years after January 1, 2027 before the parking reform starts to move permits
parameters.rationale: The benchmark parking reform is assumed to apply from the first day of the window. The delay and ramp only spread the five-year total over the years.
parameters.revisit: Set from an ordinance's effective date when a local rule is modelled.

parameters.label: Weekday departures that make a bus stop a major transit stop
parameters.rationale: The benchmark rule: a major transit stop is a fixed-guideway station, or a bus stop with at least 64 weekday departures (about every 15 minutes over 16 hours).
parameters.revisit: Only if the major-transit-stop rule changes.

parameters.label: Distance around a frequent bus stop counted as near transit
parameters.rationale: The benchmark rule: a quarter mile, straight line, for frequent bus stops.
parameters.revisit: Only if the major-transit-stop rule changes.

parameters.label: Stop-name likeness that can stand in for the reverse place check
parameters.rationale: When the reverse share fails (for example a schedule feed that also covers a neighbouring area), a pairing by place still holds if at least half the map feed's stops have a schedule stop within 50 m whose name is at least 0.8 alike (difflib ratio, lower case, punctuation removed). Renumbered stops usually keep their names.
parameters.revisit: With the place-paired feeds of each state build.

parameters.label: Share of a schedule feed's in-state stops that must sit at the map feed's stops to pair by place
parameters.rationale: A map feed whose stop ids match no schedule feed may be paired by place. Besides a shared distinctive agency-name word and half the map feed's stops within 50 m of the schedule's stops, half the schedule feed's own stops inside the state must lie within 50 m of the map feed's stops. A big agency's feed fails this against a small operator (an airport or a town shuttle) whose few stops sit at its stops.
parameters.revisit: After each state build, read the transit_feeds rows with paired_by = place.

parameters.label: Distance around a rail station counted as near transit
parameters.rationale: The benchmark rule: half a mile, straight line, for fixed-guideway stations.
parameters.revisit: Only if the major-transit-stop rule changes (the interface offers 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 mile).

parameters.label: Share of a tract's homes near a major stop that makes it transit-rich
parameters.rationale: A tract is flagged transit-rich when at least half of its housing units sit in census blocks within the benchmark distance of a major transit stop.
parameters.revisit: Test 1/4 and 3/4 once real stop data are in the pack.

parameters.label: A share of one, for the all-surface and all-structured parking variants
parameters.rationale: Sets a parking mix share to one in a bounding variant (all surface or all structured).
parameters.revisit: None; this is a bounding case.

parameters.label: A share of zero, for the all-surface and all-structured parking variants
parameters.rationale: Sets a parking mix share to zero in a bounding variant (all surface or all structured).
parameters.revisit: None; this is a bounding case.

parameters.label: Spread of voluntary parking across projects (share of the context average, either side)
parameters.rationale: Projects in one building type and transit class do not all want the same parking. With no minimum, voluntary spaces per home vary across projects evenly between average x (1 - spread) and average x (1 + spread), so some projects provide more than the old minimum (the minimum never bound them) and some far less. A study of Buffalo after it removed minimums in 2017 reported that under half of the major projects built fewer spaces than the old code required; the spread lets the model reproduce that pattern. Used only by the variant 'parking_voluntary_floor'.
parameters.revisit: Count stalls per home in a sample of approved Pennsylvania site plans, split mixed-use from residential-only.

parameters.label: Spaces per home builders provide with no minimum, apartments elsewhere
parameters.rationale: Away from frequent transit, lenders and tenants still expect about one space per home or more. Used only by the variant 'parking_provided_spaces'.
parameters.revisit: Read the Buffalo post-reform project counts and the synthesis tables.

parameters.label: Spaces per home builders provide with no minimum, apartments near frequent transit

source.citation: Research synthesis on what developers build after parking minimums are removed (eScholarship, University of California)

parameters.rationale: After minimums are removed, apartment projects near frequent transit provide well under one space per home on average, with wide variation by project. Used only by the variant 'parking_provided_spaces'.
parameters.revisit: Read the Buffalo post-reform project counts and the synthesis tables.

parameters.label: Spaces per home builders provide with no minimum, 2-4 unit buildings elsewhere
parameters.rationale: Suburban duplexes and fourplexes keep driveways; buyers and lenders expect them. Used only by the variant 'parking_provided_spaces'.
parameters.revisit: Count spaces on new 2-4 unit permits in suburbs without minimums.

parameters.label: Spaces per home builders provide with no minimum, 2-4 unit buildings near frequent transit
parameters.rationale: Small buildings on city lots near transit often give up the second space a minimum would require. Used only by the variant 'parking_provided_spaces'.
parameters.revisit: Count spaces on new 2-4 unit permits in cities without minimums.

parameters.label: Cap on conversions, as a share of the county's baseline 5+ unit permits
parameters.rationale: Converted homes compete for the same renters as new apartments.
parameters.revisit: Use Census SOMA absorption rates by metro.

parameters.label: Price paid for an obsolete office or retail building, per gross sq ft
parameters.rationale: Distressed office and retail sales are often far below replacement cost.
parameters.revisit: Use recorded sale prices of office buildings (parcel sales).

parameters.label: Conversion cost per gross sq ft (structure, systems, windows, plumbing)
parameters.rationale: Representative range for office-to-residential conversions: a simple main-street building at the low end, a deep office building needing new plumbing risers, facade work and a light well at the high end. Team judgement; not read from a cost survey.
parameters.revisit: Replace with published conversion project costs (city conversion programmes).

parameters.label: Share of feasible conversions started each year
parameters.rationale: Owners convert slowly: leases run out, financing is hard, designs take time.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on conversion counts in a city with a conversion programme.

parameters.label: Share of gross floor area that becomes rentable homes after conversion
parameters.rationale: Corridors, stairs, cores and deep interiors without windows are lost.
parameters.revisit: Use measured conversion projects' net-to-gross ratios.

parameters.label: Development fees on a converted home, as a share of the $50,000 benchmark

source.citation: Texas SB 840, 89th Legislature (2025), enrolled text, Local Government Code section 218.204: no impact fee on a conversion unless the land was already subject to one

parameters.rationale: A conversion pays building and permit fees but often fewer impact fees (Texas SB 840 bars most); the range runs from mostly waived to the full benchmark.
parameters.revisit: Set from the modelled law's fee rule.

parameters.label: Gross floor area of a building converted
parameters.rationale: From a two-storey main-street building to a mid-size office building.
parameters.revisit: Measure from parcel building areas.

parameters.label: Share of commercial parcels with an office or retail building suitable for conversion
parameters.rationale: Few commercial buildings convert well: they need a shallow floor plate, windows on enough walls and a weak current use (vacant offices, dead malls).
parameters.revisit: Use office vacancy and floor-plate screens from a city conversion study.

parameters.label: Floor area of a converted home
parameters.rationale: Conversions are mostly studios and one-bedroom homes.
parameters.revisit: Use measured conversion projects' unit mixes.

parameters.label: Equal-count bins used to estimate each input's share of the output's variance
parameters.rationale: The draws are sorted by one input and cut into this many bins with the same number of draws each. Ten bins of two hundred draws each keep the variance inside every bin well measured while still following a curved link.
parameters.revisit: Revisit if the number of draws changes a lot.

parameters.label: Share of these splits the baseline would have allowed anyway (variance or cluster rule)
parameters.rationale: Some small lots are already approved by variance or under cluster rules.
parameters.revisit: Count past variances for small lots in the parcel data.

parameters.label: Typical minimum lot in today's single-family zones
parameters.rationale: Suburban single-family zones commonly require a quarter acre or more; older boroughs less. Only lots this rule does not already let an owner split count.
parameters.revisit: Read minimum lot sizes from the municipal zoning rules table (muni_zoning_rules) where verified.

parameters.label: Share of starter homes that would have been built elsewhere in the region anyway
parameters.rationale: As the missing-middle displacement share: some buyers move from new homes elsewhere.
parameters.revisit: Compare regional permits before and after a small-lot law.

parameters.label: Floor area of a starter home
parameters.rationale: A two- or three-bedroom house on a small lot.
parameters.revisit: Use new small-lot homes' permit floor areas.

parameters.label: Share of splits that keep the existing house (versus tear down and rebuild)
parameters.rationale: Most owners split off a side or back lot; fewer sell the whole lot for a rebuild.
parameters.revisit: Use lot-split permit records (California SB 9 urban lot splits show the mix).

parameters.label: Share of a single-family home's value that is the land
parameters.rationale: Owners selling half a lot give up half the land value, not the house.
parameters.revisit: Use FHFA county land-share estimates.

parameters.label: Smallest share of a tract's homes valued near the starter-home price for lenders to find comparables
parameters.rationale: Appraisers value a new home from recent nearby sales of similar homes. Where few homes are valued within 20% of the starter-home price the appraisal (and the loan) may come in short. Below this share the tract is flagged.
parameters.revisit: Use appraisal-gap rates for new small-lot homes from lender data.

parameters.label: Smallest lot allowed for a new subdivision on single-family land (the reform)

source.citation: Texas SB 15, 89th Legislature (2025), enrolled text: in cities over 150,000 a minimum lot may not exceed 3,000 sq ft (30 ft wide, 75 ft deep) in new subdivisions of 5+ acres

parameters.rationale: The low end is Texas SB 15's 3,000 sq ft cap; 5,000 sq ft is a common small-lot zone. The reform is a choice in this range, not a measured value.
parameters.revisit: Set from the lot size a modelled state bill names.

parameters.label: Share of single-family lots the smaller minimum newly lets an owner split (no lot-size proxy)
parameters.rationale: Used only where the pack has no block lot-size proxy (lot_m2_per_unit_p25/50/75 on blocks); Testland's blocks have none.
parameters.revisit: Measure from parcel lot sizes.

parameters.label: First-year share of full take-up (starter-home lots)
parameters.rationale: Subdivision review and platting take time; take-up builds over years.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on lot-split permit ramps.

parameters.label: Years until starter-lot take-up is full
parameters.rationale: Same form as the other reforms' ramps.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on lot-split permit ramps.

parameters.label: Small homes built where a house is torn down and the lot split
parameters.rationale: A pair of small houses or a row of three townhouses on a split lot.
parameters.revisit: Use small-lot subdivision records.

parameters.label: Price of a starter home as a share of the tract's median home value
parameters.rationale: A smaller home on a smaller lot sells below the typical home nearby.
parameters.revisit: Use sale prices of small-lot new homes.

parameters.label: Share of feasible lots split each year
parameters.rationale: Lot splits are rare even where legal: early California SB 9 years saw very few applications per eligible lot. Near the missing-middle redevelopment rate.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on lot-split permits after Texas SB 15 or California SB 9.

parameters.label: Years after January 1, 2027 before starter-lot permits respond
parameters.rationale: Assumed in force on the first day of the window, like the benchmarks.
parameters.revisit: Set from a bill's effective date when one is modelled.

parameters.label: Subdivision and utility cost per new lot (survey, plat, engineering, laterals, curb cut)
parameters.rationale: A minor subdivision needs a survey, plan review and recording, and each new lot its own water and sewer laterals, tap fees and driveway. Team judgement.
parameters.revisit: Use municipal subdivision fee schedules and utility tap fees.

parameters.label: Land cost as a share of development cost, pro-forma cross-check
parameters.rationale: Used only by the pro-forma cross-check of the fee and parking reforms: a project pencils where its value covers development cost, the builder's return and land. Land is often a tenth to a quarter of total cost.
parameters.revisit: Source land shares from published development pro formas or land sales.

parameters.label: Pareto shape of the open top rent and value bracket, pro-forma cross-check
parameters.rationale: Break-evens for new buildings often fall inside the open top ACS bracket ($3,500+ rent, $2,000,000+ value). The cross-check spreads that bracket as a Pareto tail with this shape instead of treating it as zero. Larger values mean a thinner tail. Rents are less spread out than incomes, so the central value sits above typical income-tail shapes.
parameters.revisit: Fit from tract rent microdata (ACS PUMS) for Pennsylvania metros.

parameters.label: Medium-run supply response to a change in profit per unit

source.citation: Albert Saiz (2010), "The Geographic Determinants of Housing Supply", Quarterly Journal of Economics 125(3), 1253-1296, Table VI (metro areas with population over 500,000)
Nathaniel Baum-Snow and Lu Han (2024), "The Microgeography of Housing Supply", Journal of Political Economy 132(6), 1897-1946, abstract

parameters.rationale: Percent change in permitted units for a 1% change in the value-to-cost margin. Published metropolitan housing-supply elasticities for older northeastern metros mostly sit between about 0.5 and 2; 1.0 is a neutral central value until the cross-check job is run.
parameters.revisit: Cite the metro elasticity study and the 2024 tract-level study after reading them; cross-check with the planned elasticity cross-check (literature values against a long-difference estimate from permits and prices).

parameters.label: Metro housing supply elasticity, Philadelphia PA-NJ (Saiz 2010)

source.citation: Albert Saiz (2010), "The Geographic Determinants of Housing Supply", Quarterly Journal of Economics 125(3), 1253-1296, Table VI (metro areas with population over 500,000)

parameters.rationale: Evidence, not a model input: Table VI lists Philadelphia at 1.65 and the paper's population-weighted metro average is 1.75. It brackets the central medium-run elasticity from above; Saiz measures the long-run price elasticity of the housing stock, not of permits.
parameters.revisit: Use with the planned elasticity cross-check to set the range of supply.elasticity_medium_run.

parameters.label: Metro housing supply elasticity, Pittsburgh PA (Saiz 2010)

source.citation: Albert Saiz (2010), "The Geographic Determinants of Housing Supply", Quarterly Journal of Economics 125(3), 1253-1296, Table VI (metro areas with population over 500,000)

parameters.rationale: Evidence, not a model input: Table VI lists Pittsburgh at 1.20 (Allentown 1.86, Harrisburg 1.63, Scranton 1.62). Pennsylvania metros sit between about 1.2 and 1.9 in the long run.
parameters.revisit: Use with the planned elasticity cross-check to set the range of supply.elasticity_medium_run.

parameters.label: Average neighbourhood housing-unit supply elasticity (Baum-Snow and Han 2024)

source.citation: Nathaniel Baum-Snow and Lu Han (2024), "The Microgeography of Housing Supply", Journal of Political Economy 132(6), 1897-1946, abstract

parameters.rationale: Evidence, not a model input: across urban U.S. tracts, floor-space and unit supply elasticities average about 0.5 and 0.3. Read from the abstract. It brackets the medium-run elasticity from below, since a single tract can push demand onto its neighbours.
parameters.revisit: Read the full article and record the table; use with the planned elasticity cross-check.

parameters.label: Value of a newly built unit above the area's median, as a share
parameters.rationale: Value per new unit (V) starts from the county median home value (or median gross rent, for rented building types) read from ACS brackets. New homes sell and rent above the median of the existing stock, so V adds this premium.
parameters.revisit: Compare new-construction sale prices (Census SOC) with ACS county medians.

parameters.label: Share of a cost saving that reaches the decision to build
parameters.rationale: Part of any cut in fees or parking cost is captured by landowners as higher land prices rather than turning into more homes. Half is a neutral start; the range is wide because the evidence on who bears fees is mixed.
parameters.revisit: Read the evidence on fee incidence and narrow the range.

parameters.label: Most extra 5+ unit permits a county can absorb, as a share of its baseline 5+ unit permits

source.citation: Evidence library entry ev.tod.chicago_freemark: Yonah Freemark (2020), "Upzoning Chicago", Urban Affairs Review 56(3), abstract

parameters.rationale: New apartments must be rented: lenders and builders pace projects to regional demand, so a zoning change near stations moves only part of a county's apartment pipeline in five years. A county with no recent 5+ unit permits gets no TOD units.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on station-area upzonings: added 5+ permits against the region's pipeline.

parameters.label: Premium over current value a mid-rise builder pays to assemble a site
parameters.rationale: Assembling several lots means paying holdouts above market; upzoning also raises asking prices (Chicago station-area land prices rose after upzoning).
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on station-area land sales after upzoning.

parameters.label: Chance a site redeveloped under TOD would have been redeveloped at today's floor area anyway in 2027-2031
parameters.rationale: The homes today's rules allow on a site are in the baseline only if the site would have been redeveloped in the window anyway. The authorizations subtracted from the reform's on a redeveloped site are this chance x the apartments today's floor area allows there. Sites near stations do turn over, but most that pencil only at the upzoned height would not be rebuilt at today's height, so the chance is well below one.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from station-area permits on parcels before and after upzonings.

parameters.label: Floor area ratio allowed today near major stops (before the reform)
parameters.rationale: Most land near Pennsylvania stations is zoned for houses, rowhouses or low-rise commercial, roughly FAR 0.4-1.4. Only floor area above this counts as added by the reform; the rest was allowed already (and is in the baseline).
parameters.revisit: Read base-district FARs near stations from municipal zoning codes.

parameters.label: Share of land near a major stop that could be rebuilt as mid-rise, rural tracts
parameters.rationale: Few rural tracts are near a major stop, and little of that land suits mid-rise.
parameters.revisit: Measure soft-site shares from parcel data near PA stations.

parameters.label: Share of land near a major stop that could be rebuilt as mid-rise, suburban tracts
parameters.rationale: Suburban station areas mix parking lots and strip retail (good sites) with single-family streets that rarely assemble into mid-rise sites.
parameters.revisit: Measure soft-site shares from parcel data near PA stations.

parameters.label: Share of land near a major stop that could be rebuilt as mid-rise, urban tracts
parameters.rationale: Block land near a station also holds parks, schools, churches, recent or large buildings, historic districts and small lots that cannot be assembled. Only a minority of it is a realistic mid-rise site within a decade.
parameters.revisit: Measure soft-site shares from parcel data (assessed improvement-to-land ratio) near PA stations.

parameters.label: End of the morning peak window (hour, exclusive)
parameters.rationale: Morning peak window 7:00 to 9:00. Windows use whole hours, because departures are counted per hour.
parameters.revisit: Only if the peak window definition changes.

parameters.label: Start of the morning peak window (hour of the service day)
parameters.rationale: Morning peak window 7:00 to 9:00 (start inclusive, end exclusive): the two busiest commuting hours in most U.S. schedules.
parameters.revisit: Only if the peak window definition changes.

parameters.label: Longest average scheduled headway that makes a bus stop frequent, in both peaks
parameters.rationale: A bus stop is a major stop under the walkshed rule when buses leave the same platform (one side of the street) on average at least every 15 minutes in both weekday peak windows, all routes added. Fifteen minutes is the usual frequent-service line in transit planning and in state transit-density laws; the daily benchmark rule (64 departures) is its all-day cousin.
parameters.revisit: Test 10 and 20 minutes by rebuilding the table with an override; revisit if a Pennsylvania bill defines frequent service.

parameters.label: Heading difference beyond which a trip leaves a bus pole the other way
parameters.rationale: Peak departures are counted per platform-level stop with all routes added, because GTFS direction_id is defined route by route. A pole is split into two sides only when some trips leave it heading more than 120 degrees away from its main heading (the bearing to each trip's next stop; main heading = the 30-degree sector with the most trips). 120 rather than 90 degrees leaves room for routes that turn at the next corner, which are still on the same side of the street.
parameters.revisit: Check split poles by hand on a map in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh (loops and terminals).

parameters.label: End of the afternoon peak window (hour, exclusive)
parameters.rationale: Afternoon peak window 16:00 to 18:00.
parameters.revisit: Only if the peak window definition changes.

parameters.label: Start of the afternoon peak window (hour of the service day)
parameters.rationale: Afternoon peak window 16:00 to 18:00 (4 to 6 pm).
parameters.revisit: Only if the peak window definition changes.

parameters.label: Share of a mid-rise site the building covers
parameters.rationale: Mid-rise buildings cover most of the lot; setbacks, courtyards and access take the rest.
parameters.revisit: Check against recent mid-rise site plans in Pennsylvania.

parameters.label: Floor area ratio of the low-rise TOD prototype (variant)
parameters.rationale: Three to four storeys with surface parking cover less of the lot than a mid-rise with a garage. Used only by the variant 'tod_lowrise'.
parameters.revisit: Measure from site plans of recent walk-up apartment projects.

parameters.label: Construction cost per sq ft of the low-rise TOD prototype (variant)
parameters.rationale: A wood-frame walk-up has no elevator core, concrete podium or garage, so it costs less per square foot than the mid-rise (multifamily.hard_cost_per_sqft). Used only by the variant 'tod_lowrise'.
parameters.revisit: Price from published construction cost guides for garden and walk-up apartments.

parameters.label: Storeys of the low-rise TOD prototype (variant)
parameters.rationale: A three- to four-storey wood-frame walk-up with surface parking: the building small-town and rural station areas can support. Used only by the variant 'tod_lowrise'.
parameters.revisit: Check against recent walk-up apartment permits in Vermont and rural Pennsylvania.

parameters.label: Smallest number of existing homes per acre used to price a site
parameters.rationale: A site is priced as its existing homes x their value. Land near stations with few homes (shops, parking lots) still costs something; this floor prices it like a few houses per acre.
parameters.revisit: Replace with assessed land values near stations.

parameters.label: Share of a mid-rise building's floor area that is apartments
parameters.rationale: Corridors, stairs, lobbies and services take 12-25% of gross floor area.
parameters.revisit: Check against published mid-rise efficiency ratios.

parameters.label: Share of TOD units that are new to the region (not moved from elsewhere in it)
parameters.rationale: Some apartments built near stations would have been built elsewhere in the same region anyway; the reform only moves them. Those are not counted. The range is deliberately wide, and this is a headline caveat.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from regional 5+ unit permits before and after station-area upzonings.

parameters.label: Rent of a new mid-rise apartment as a multiple of the tract's two-bedroom median
parameters.rationale: New buildings with amenities near transit rent above the existing stock, most of which is decades old.
parameters.revisit: Compare new-lease asking rents with ACS medians near PA stations.

parameters.label: First-year mid-rise permits as a share of the full yearly rate
parameters.rationale: Mid-rise projects take one to three years from site control to a building permit.
parameters.revisit: Check against permit timing after station-area upzonings.

parameters.label: Years for mid-rise permits to reach the full yearly rate
parameters.rationale: Larger projects need assembly, design, financing and approvals; slower than ADUs.
parameters.revisit: Check against permit timing after station-area upzonings.

parameters.label: Share of feasible mid-rise sites permitted each year

source.citation: Evidence library entry ev.tod.chicago_freemark: Yonah Freemark (2020), "Upzoning Chicago", Urban Affairs Review 56(3), abstract

parameters.rationale: Station-area upzonings are taken up slowly: Chicago's found no detectable rise in permits within about five years, while land prices rose. A few percent of feasible sites a year keeps five-year take-up well below capacity.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on station-area upzonings with permit counts (Minneapolis, Seattle, Chicago full paper).

parameters.label: Two-bedroom rent as a multiple of median gross rent, where the two-bedroom median is blank
parameters.rationale: In Pennsylvania tracts the two-bedroom median is close to the all-units median gross rent.
parameters.revisit: Compute from ACS B25031 tracts that report both.

parameters.label: Years after January 1, 2027 before mid-rise permits near stops start to respond
parameters.rationale: The benchmark reform is assumed to be in force on the first day of the window; the one-to-three-year path from site control to a permit is in the ramp (tod.ramp_first_year_share).
parameters.revisit: Set from a bill's effective date when a bill is modelled.

parameters.label: Share of a state by-right multi-family district's land that lies inside the TOD walk distance
parameters.rationale: Massachusetts already zones districts for multi-family homes by right near transit (MBTA Communities, Section 3A). Upzoning that land again adds no new mid-rise sites, so the TOD reform takes it out. A district counted as inside a station area can still reach past the half-mile circle, so only this share of its acres is taken out, never more than the tract's land near a stop. Read only by variant tod_ma_acre_share (and by a pack that has a district table but no 3A capacity table). Since M1b the benchmark compares the 3A parcels' own modeled capacity (mbta_3a_capacity_tract) with the prototype on the same land instead.
parameters.revisit: Replaced in the benchmark by the 3A capacity comparison; kept for the variant bridge.

parameters.label: Share of a state's bus stops with measured service needed to show a statewide TOD range
parameters.rationale: Bus stops whose scheduled departures were not counted (no readable feed) have unknown service, and nothing bounds what they would add. When at least half of the National Transit Map's bus stops in a state were measured, the measured part is the larger part and the statewide range is shown with a "partial footprint" label. Below half, the unknown part is the larger part: the statewide range and percent change are suppressed and only the measured contribution is reported, labelled. Rail stops count as measured (major by mode). A rule for display, not sampled.
parameters.revisit: If a bound for unmeasured agencies (for example from published route headways) becomes available.

parameters.label: Floor area ratio allowed near major stops after the reform

source.citation: Evidence library entry ev.tod.california_sb79_2025: California Senate Bill 79 (2025), state floors of 80-120 homes per acre and 55-75 ft near stops

parameters.rationale: The reform's definition, not an uncertain number. FAR 2.5 with 850 sq ft apartments and 82% net floor area is about 105 homes per acre, inside California SB 79's 80-120 per acre floors. Change it to study a stronger or weaker upzoning; 0 (or anything at or below today's allowed FAR) adds nothing.
parameters.revisit: Revisit if a Pennsylvania transit-density bill sets its own floors.

parameters.label: Storeys allowed near major stops after the reform

source.citation: Evidence library entry ev.tod.california_sb79_2025: California Senate Bill 79 (2025), height floors of 55, 65 and 75 ft

parameters.rationale: The reform's definition. Five storeys (about 55-65 ft) is the common wood-over- podium mid-rise. The usable floor area ratio is the lower of the FAR limit and storeys x lot coverage.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with a Pennsylvania bill text.

parameters.label: Width counted on each side of a reached street or path
parameters.rationale: Land counts as reached when it lies within 50 m of a street or path that is within the walking distance: about one lot depth (typical Pennsylvania lots are 30 to 60 m deep). Wider buffers fill large blocks; narrower ones leave block interiors out.
parameters.revisit: Compare with parcel depths near stations once parcel data cover more counties.

parameters.label: Smallest network piece a stop may join
parameters.rationale: A stop whose nearest network nodes belong to a connected piece shorter than one mile (1,609 m) in total is on a fragment (a platform or a path the map does not link to streets). The network is treated as incomplete there and the stop uses its straight-line circle, flagged as fallback.
parameters.revisit: Check fallback stops by hand; lower it if complete small towns are being flagged.

parameters.label: Farthest a stop may be from the walking network to join it
parameters.rationale: A stop joins every walkable network node within 80 m, starting at its straight-line distance. Stops sit on streets or platforms, so 80 m is ample; a larger value would let walks jump across rail cuts and highways.
parameters.revisit: Check the stops that fall back to straight lines by hand.
